newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Irish president appears favorite for U.N. rights post.
newsitem.headline: Irish president appears favorite for U.N. rights post.

text.p: Irish President Mary Robinson appears to be the main candidate for the top U.N. human rights job after the United Nations said on Friday her chief competitor had not been offered the post.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard told a news briefing that Sonia Picado, Costa Rica's ambassador to the United States, who spoke to Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday was not offered the job of U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights.

He refused to say whether Robinson would be named to the Geneva-based post, although she and Picado for weeks had been the leading candidates. Eckhard said an official announcement would be made by the end of July.
Picado, an author and former judge and law school dean who has substantial backing from developing countries, said she had been offered alternative jobs related to human rights.
It was her second visit with him, the first one being on April 3. Robinson spoke to Annan in New York on May 23 but revealed little of substance about their talks.

Asked about Picado, Eckhard confirmed "that she had not been offered the high commissioner for human rights post but that the secretary-general did indicate his interest in her for another post which I am not at liberty to describe."

"He cast a wide net and he asked everyone to review names but as far as I know the door is open to new candidates but I am not aware of any new candidates coming forward," Eckhard said. He added that he did not necessarily agree that Robinson was the only candidate at this time.
But according to diplomats Annan was searching for a qualified woman for the post.

While Finland's former defence minister, Elizabeth Rehn, had expressed interest, they said Robinson was the stronger candidate. But Because of Rehn's candidacy Europeans have not endorsed anyone, although the United States and Britain are known to have told Annan of their support for Robinson.
If Robinson is selected, Annan may run into trouble in the General Assembly, which has to approve the sensitive post and is dominated by Third World nations.

The position, first proposed nearly 50 years ago, became vacant after Jose Ayala Lasso resigned in March as the first human rights commissioner to become Ecuador's foreign minister. He was appointed in 1994 for four years.
In the interim, the job is being carried out by Briton Ralph Zacklin, a deputy to the U.N. under-secretary general for legal affairs.
Robinson, a lawyer and human rights expert, does not end her seven-year term as president of Ireland until December although there are reports she would be available in November.

Annan had considerd a deputy high commissioner post, diplomats said, and human rights groups want him to appoint a rights coordinator in New York. Picado said she did not want to be a deputy, explaining: If I am not the high commissioner, I am not sure that I want to accept another post." But she said she might consider some kind of coordinating post.
